The Network traffic page merges them live from all gateway pods: a graph of sandboxes and destinations, and a table with verdicts and reasons. A not-allowlisted denial raises a network-access request on the task, so the agent’s need shows up in the inbox. How to allow or deny hosts: Network access.
data.rule-changes-reach-running-sandboxes#Rul: Rules live in PostgreSQL. A change is pushed through the control plane to every gateway pod (PolicyWatch) and applies to the next connection, typically within a second, without restarting the run. Removing a host closes the run’s open tunnels to it. The per-run NetworkPolicies are re-rendered when rules or the referenced Services change, and manual edits to them are overwritten.
data.traffic-paths#Traffic paths: Traffic Path Enforced by Agent channel Direct to the control plane agent port, mTLS NetworkPolicy HTTP(S) to external hosts Egress proxy (CONNECT or plain HTTP forwarding) Egress rules in the proxy; the NetworkPolicy lets the sandbox reach only the gateway Git Git proxy on the gateway Git proxy In-cluster services Direct, as cluster-service rules Generated NetworkPolicy DNS Denied NetworkPolicy The pod spec sets HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY to the gateway’s ClusterIP and NO_PROXY plus hostAliases for allowed cluster services, so no name needs DNS.
data.what-the-proxy-checks#What the proxy che: Check Denial reason The source pod IP belongs to a known run unknown-source CONNECT host:port matches an allow rule of the run (exact host or *.suffix, port, default 443) not-allowlisted (403) The TLS ClientHello names the same host (SNI) sni-mismatch (tunnel closed) None of the host’s addresses is private, loopback, link-local, CGNAT or a cluster address; the proxy resolves the name itself private-destination The destination is a name, not an IP literal ip-literal Plain HTTP (GET http://…) only for rules with port 80 set explicitly denied Until a gateway pod has received its first policy snapshot it denies everything and reports not ready, so a rollout never lets traffic through unchecked. The proxy does not intercept TLS: it sees the host, the port and the TLS handshake, not paths or headers.

data:
Sandboxes clone, fetch and push only through the gateway’s Git smart-HTTP proxy. The proxy holds the forge credential, restricts what a run may push, checks every pushed commit and records every push.
flowchart LR R["Runtime / git
(sandbox)"] -- "https://gateway:8443/git/DF-12.git
no credential" --> P["Git proxy"] P -- "source IP → run → task" --> P P -- "checks, push record" --> CP["Control plane"] P -- "forge credential" --> F["Forge"]
data.allowed-ref-updates#Allowed ref updates:
A push is forwarded only if every ref update is:
Ref Allowed update refs/heads/factory/task/ create or fast-forward refs/heads/factory/wip/ create, update or delete (the WIP snapshot) Anything else (another branch, a tag, a force-push, another task’s branch) rejects the whole push before the forge is contacted. Git prints the reason, prefixed with df:.
data.credential-injection#Credential injectio:
The proxy forwards to the project’s repository URL with the project’s forge credential. It drops any Authorization header from the client, and never returns the credential to the client or writes it to a log. The runtime’s Git configuration has no credential helper, so nothing in the sandbox could hold a credential either.
http:// repositories get no route unless the instance setting forge.allowPlainHttp is on; the sandbox always talks HTTPS to the gateway.
data.endpoint-and-caller#Endpoint and caller: The proxy serves https://:8443/git/.git with a certificate from the instance CA (fetch with protocol v2 and partial clone, and push). It identifies the run by the source pod IP; an unknown source, or a path naming another task than the run’s, gets 403. Until the gateway has its first policy snapshot it answers 503, which the runtime retries.
data.push-checks#Push checks:
Before forwarding, the proxy checks the commits a push adds (commits already on the forge are not checked again):
Check Finding Configurable per project Secret scan df:secret-scan: rule, path, line and a masked preview; the secret itself is never stored or logged mode approval (default) or reject Commit identity df:identity: author and committer must be the instance’s commit identity no, always enforced Protected paths df:protected-path: a change below a protected glob; .dark-factory/** is always protected globs (default CI workflow directories and CODEOWNERS) and mode Blob size df:blob-too-large: a file larger than the limit limit (default 5 MiB) and mode Linear history df:merge-commit on or off (default off) Commit limit df:push-too-large: more than 10,000 commits no Push size df:push-too-large (HTTP 413): a push body above the maximum (default 256 MiB) instance setting Pushes to the WIP branch get only the secret scan and the size limit, always rejecting.
Approval mode. A task-branch push rejected only by approval-mode findings raises a push-check-exception request in the inbox, listing the findings. Approving it creates exceptions for exactly these findings, and the agent’s next push passes them; findings in reject mode stay rejected. The agent gets a message with the masked findings either way. Board members change the modes on the project’s Push checks tab.
data.push-records#Push records: Every push attempt is stored with the control plane before the client gets an answer: run, task, ref updates with old and new SHA, verdict, reasons, bytes and duration. A push is recorded as forwarding before anything reaches the forge. If the record cannot be stored within 5 seconds, the push is rejected (df:audit-unavailable).
data.upstream-failures#Upstream failures: Proxy answer Meaning 503 The forge is unreachable or timed out, or the gateway has no snapshot yet; the runtime retries 502 The forge rejected the credential (401, 403) or answered with another error; not retried Reference: Git hardening in the runtime.

data:
Dark Factory treats agents like employees: you give them a project and a role, assign tasks, answer their questions and review their pull requests in your forge. Everything happens in the web UI; creating tasks and answering questions also works on a phone.
flowchart LR C[Credential references] --> P[Projects] C --> PE[Personas] P --> T[Tasks] PE --> T T --> R[Requests] T --> PR[Draft pull request] Set up in this order:
Credentials, projects and personas: references to the forge and harness credentials, the repositories and the agents. Tasks: describe the work, follow the transcript, send messages, stop or cancel. Requests: answer questions and decide approvals. Network access: allow the hosts agents need.
A sandbox reaches no external host until a rule allows it (see Egress gateway). Board members manage the rules on the Egress rules page and watch the traffic on the Network traffic page.
data.allow-a-host-an-agent-needs#Allow a host:
When an agent hits a blocked host, the gateway reports it and a network-access request appears in the Requests inbox, with the host and port. Three ways to allow it:
From the request: approve it and pick the scope (task, project or everywhere). The agent gets the decision as a message; its retry succeeds. From the traffic view: on a blocked row or graph node choose Allow, then the scope. On the Egress rules page: New egress rule, host, port and scope. Any new host rule settles the pending requests it covers.
data.kinds-of-rules#Kinds of rules: Rule Allows Scopes Host (http-host) CONNECT to a host name (registry.npmjs.org) or all subdomains (*.npmjs.org) on one port (default 443; 80 only when set) instance (“Everywhere”), project, task Cluster service (cluster-service) direct connections to a Kubernetes Service, for example a build cache; reachable by its DNS name without DNS (hostAliases) instance, project Deny rule nothing; it silences requests for a host that should never be allowed (below) instance A run may use the union of the instance rules, its project’s rules and its task’s rules. A new rule applies to the next connection of running sandboxes within about a second; no restart needed. Cluster services must be in a namespace the chart allows (clusterTargets).
data.network-traffic-page#Network traffic pag: The page shows live connections from all gateway pods: a graph of sandboxes and destinations on the left (blocked edges dashed red), the events on the right, newest first. Filter by domain or IP, by verdict (All, Blocked, Allowed) and under Advanced by persona, sandbox, project or task. Pause stops the stream. A row’s details show what the gateway records: method, status, duration, bytes, SNI, source, gateway pod, the reason and the matching rule. Request contents inside TLS are not inspected. Events live in memory only; a restarted gateway pod starts empty.
data.silence-a-host-that-should-never-be-allo:
Some harnesses send telemetry to hosts you will never allow (for example Claude Code to http-intake.logs.us5.datadoghq.com:443). Every run raises the same request for it. A deny rule ends that:
Open Egress rules and choose New egress rule. Select Deny. “Applies to” and Port are disabled: a deny rule covers every project and every port. Enter the host (http-intake.logs.us5.datadoghq.com, or *.datadoghq.com for all subdomains) and choose Add deny rule. Shortcuts: Deny always on a network-access request in the inbox (denies the request and creates a rule for its exact host) and Deny always on a blocked row of the network traffic page.
What a deny rule does:
Case Result A run connects to the host Still blocked (not-allowlisted). The gateway is unchanged. The gateway reports the denial No request is raised. An agent asks for the host (request_approval) The agent gets “denied by instance policy” and nothing is stored. Pending requests for matching hosts exist They are denied on creation, as the system principal, with a comment naming the rule. An allow rule for the host exists The allow rule still wins: the deny rule only silences requests. Traffic page Matching rows show “Deny rule” and offer no actions. Open pages pick up a new rule when the stream reconnects. Deleting the rule makes the host raise requests again. Creating and deleting are audited as egress_deny_rule.create and egress_deny_rule.delete.

data:
Agents ask before they guess, and they cannot grant themselves anything. Both show up as requests: in the Requests inbox (the count is on every page) and as cards on the task’s timeline.
Kind Raised by You decide Question the agent, with up to 5 suggested answers tap a suggested answer or write one network-access approval the gateway when a host is blocked, or the agent with a reason approve for the task, the project or everywhere; deny; or Deny always (Network access) push-check-exception approval the Git proxy when a push hits findings in approval mode approve exactly these findings for this task, or deny (Git proxy)
data.blocking-and-non-blocking#Blocking and n: A blocking question stops the agent’s work until it is answered. If nobody answers within the idle deadline, the run ends and the task becomes blocked; your answer later queues the task again and the next run continues with it. A non-blocking request lets the agent carry on, for example with a fallback.
data.what-happens-on-a-decision#What happens: The control plane applies an approved action itself (it creates the egress rule or the push exception); the agent never does. The decision reaches the agent as a message at its next turn, including your comment. Identical pending requests of a task are merged; a task can have at most 20 pending requests. Completing or cancelling a task closes its pending requests. Raising, deciding and closing are audited. Request texts come from the agent and are shown as plain text: links are not followed and no HTML is rendered.

data: Everything below is configured in the web UI by a board member and stored in the database. Every create and edit is audited with the old and new values.
data.credential-references#Credential referen:
Dark Factory never stores secret values. A credential reference names a Kubernetes Secret in the instance namespace and a key in it; the control plane reads the value when it uses it.
Create the Secret, for example kubectl -n dark-factory create secret generic claude-token --from-file=token=. Credentials → New credential reference: a name, the Secret name and the key. Two kinds of credentials are referenced:
Credential Used by Reaches the sandbox Forge credential (a token of a bot account) the forge plugins (API) and the Git proxy never Harness credential (for example a Claude subscription token, CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN) the agent harness yes, in memory over the agent channel, at every connect
data.personas#Personas:
A persona is an agent with a role. Personas → New persona:
Field Meaning Name Shown in the task list and transcript, for example “Linus”. System prompt The role and the working rules of this agent. Harness The coding agent that runs in the sandbox (claude-code). Model Optional; empty uses the harness default. Harness credential The credential reference the harness logs in with. Every task is assigned to one persona; the persona’s harness, model and prompt apply to all runs of the task.
data.projects#Projects:
Projects → New project:
Field Meaning Name, Key Display name and the task key prefix (DF → tasks DF-1, DF-2, …). The key is 2–10 capital letters or digits, starting with a letter, and cannot change later. Repository URL HTTPS clone URL. Its host selects the forge plugin; the hint below the field names it. Base branch Where task branches start and pull requests point to. Issue tracker URL Optional. Sandbox image The image the agent works in. It needs git and a shell; the runtime and the harness are mounted into it. Adapter command Optional. Replaces the instance’s harness image for this project (a harness installed in the sandbox image). Forge credential The credential reference for the forge. The Push checks tab sets what the Git proxy checks for this project: protected paths, secret scan and blob size, each in mode approval or reject, and whether merge commits are allowed.
The project list shows the number of queued, running, waiting and done tasks per project.

data: A task is a piece of work for one persona in one project. Its code lives on the branch factory/task/; the agent opens a draft pull request with its first commit and you review it in your forge.
data.create-a-task#Create a task: New task (the green button) opens the composer: pick the project, describe the work, pick the persona and send. The task gets the next key of the project (DF-12) and starts as soon as a run slot is free. Without a title, the first sentence of the description is used until the agent sets a better one; you can rename a task at any time.
data.follow-and-steer-it#Follow and steer it:
The task view has three columns: the task list, the transcript and the details.
Transcript: the agent’s messages and tool calls (commands, file reads and edits) live, as they happen. Messages: type into the message box at any time. A message reaches the agent at the next turn boundary, without restarting anything; while it waits it is shown as queued and can be edited or removed. A message to a finished task reopens it. Details: what the agent is doing now, the pull request and issue links, project, persona, branch and the list of runs with model and token usage.
data.status#Status: Status Meaning queued Work is pending; a run starts when a slot is free or the resume time has passed running A run is working on it waiting The agent finished its turn and waits for you; the sandbox stays alive for a while (runs.keepAliveSeconds) blocked A blocking question or approval was not answered in time; answering resumes the task in_review The agent called complete_task; the pull request is ready for review rate_limited The model provider’s usage limit was hit; the task resumes automatically at the shown time limit_reached A budget of the run, or the harness’s token or turn limit, was reached; a message continues it completed Marked done by a human cancelled Cancelled by a human failed The run failed and automatic retries are exhausted The list’s filters group them: Active, Waiting (waiting, blocked, in_review, limit_reached) and Done (completed, failed).
data.stop-mark-done-cancel#Stop, mark done, c:
From the status menu in the details:
Action Effect Stop (also the stop button in the message box) Ends the current run; the agent finalizes (pushes, snapshots) and the task waits for your next message. Mark done The task becomes completed and its pull request is marked ready for review. Cancel task Stops the run, discards queued messages and closes pending requests. The pull request stays as it is.
